You are a debugging assistant. You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure, and several recent issue reports that have been pre-filtered by an external semantic retrieval model (SBERT) to be the most relevant to this failure among recent reports.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– likely-relevant recent bug reports,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.
Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

messages.content:
Title: Diagnosis
Details:
- What the test does: NormalDistributionTest.testMath280 constructs a standard normal distribution and calls inverseCumulativeProbability(0.9772498680518209). For a standard normal, this p corresponds to x = 2.0 (since Φ(2) ≈ 0.9772498680518209), so the test expects the method to return 2.0 without error.

- How inverseCumulativeProbability is implemented:
  - NormalDistributionImpl.inverseCumulativeProbability(p) delegates to AbstractContinuousDistribution.inverseCumulativeProbability(p) for 0 < p < 1.
  - AbstractContinuousDistribution.inverseCumulativeProbability solves for the root of f(x) = cumulativeProbability(x) − p using bracketing and a root solver:
    - It builds f(x) using NormalDistributionImpl.cumulativeProbability.
    - It asks UnivariateRealSolverUtils.bracket(...) to find a bracketing interval [a, b] with a sign change (i.e., f(a) and f(b) of opposite sign), starting from an initial guess given by NormalDistributionImpl.getInitialDomain(p).

- Values in this particular call:
  - mean = 0, standardDeviation = 1.
  - p = 0.9772498680518209.
  - getInitialDomain(p) returns 1.0 (mean + sd since p > 0.5).
  - getDomainLowerBound(p) = mean = 0.0 (since p ≥ 0.5).
  - getDomainUpperBound(p) = Double.MAX_VALUE.
  - The bracketing routine starts at a = b = 1. On the first expansion, it sets a = 0 and b = 2.
  - For a standard normal with this p, f(2) = Φ(2) − p = 0. Therefore, one endpoint (b = 2) is exactly a root.

- Where it goes wrong:
  - UnivariateRealSolverUtils.bracket tries to expand until f(a) and f(b) have opposite signs, using the loop condition (fa * fb > 0.0).
  - The loop stops as soon as fa * fb ≤ 0, which correctly includes the case where one endpoint is exactly a root (product = 0).
  - However, immediately after the loop, the code checks if (fa * fb >= 0.0) and, if true, throws a ConvergenceException. This treats the valid case of an endpoint being exactly a root (fa*fb == 0.0) as a failure instead of accepting it as a valid bracket. This is the crux of the bug.
  - In this test, because f(2) evaluates to 0 for the chosen p, the method incorrectly throws ConvergenceException even though a valid bracket (indeed, an exact root at the endpoint) has been found.

- Why the exception isn’t recovered:
  - AbstractContinuousDistribution.inverseCumulativeProbability catches ConvergenceException and tries to see if the domain endpoints are effectively roots by checking |f(lowerBound)| and |f(upperBound)| < 1e-6. Here, lowerBound = 0 and upperBound = Double.MAX_VALUE; neither is near the true root at x = 2, so these checks fail and the exception is rethrown as MathException, causing the test to fail.

- Summary:
  - The failure is not due to the normal distribution’s CDF/inverse logic itself, but due to a bracketing utility bug: after bracketing, the code incorrectly rejects intervals where one endpoint is an exact root by using a “>= 0” check instead of “> 0.” This leads inverseCumulativeProbability to throw when p exactly matches Φ at some x (here x = 2), even though the solver had effectively found the root at an endpoint.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
